options.C: Temporal artery scanner
options.D: Digital electronic thermometer

explanation: Mercury is a toxic heavy metal, leading healthcare facilities worldwide to replace glass-mercury devices with safer digital options. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h4)

question: What technology do tympanic thermometers use to measure body temperature quickly?

options.A: Chemical color change strips placed on the skin
options.B: Expansion of colored alcohol inside a glass tube
options.C: Infrared radiation emitted by the eardrum
options.D: Electrical resistance of a metal wire tip

explanation: Tympanic thermometers capture thermal infrared energy coming directly from the tympanic membrane without needing prolonged contact. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h4)

question: Which body site generally gives a temperature reading closest to true internal core body temperature?

options.A: Rectal site
options.B: Forehead site
options.C: Axillary site
options.D: Skin surface

explanation: Because it is enclosed deep within the body cavity, the rectum is protected from environmental air and provides the most accurate core reading. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h5)

question: How do armpit (axillary) temperature readings typically compare to internal core measurements?

options.A: They fluctuate wildly based on room lighting alone
options.B: They are usually slightly lower than core temperature
options.C: They are always significantly higher than oral readings
options.D: They match rectal temperature without any difference

explanation: The armpit is an external surface exposed to surrounding air, making axillary readings about 0.5°C lower than core values. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why might a woman's body temperature register slightly higher during the latter half of her menstrual cycle or early pregnancy?

options.A: Decreased metabolic rate forces the body to store extra environmental heat
options.B: Higher fluid intake causes temporary internal friction in the blood vessels
options.C: Enlarged milk ducts in the breasts produce constant thermal energy
options.D: Increased progesterone levels after ovulation raise the baseline set point

explanation: Progesterone is a hormone that naturally shifts the body's baseline temperature slightly upward after ovulation. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h6)

question: A mother just finished drinking hot tea when you enter the ward to take her oral temperature. What is the best action?

options.A: Record the high reading immediately as a sign of impending fever
options.B: Wait about fifteen minutes before taking the oral temperature
options.C: Subtract one degree from whatever number the thermometer shows
options.D: Switch immediately to taking her temperature on her bare leg

explanation: Hot or cold drinks temporarily alter the temperature of the mouth, so clinicians must wait for the mouth to return to baseline. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of using disposable probe covers on clinical thermometers?

options.A: To make the thermometer tip slide into body cavities faster
options.B: To prevent passing germs from one patient to another
options.C: To keep the electronic screen from getting scratched
options.D: To prevent the plastic from melting during hot weather

explanation: Disposable covers create a physical barrier that stops bacteria and viruses from passing from one patient to another. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which of the following practices is NOT recommended when caring for clinical thermometers?

options.A: Wiping reusable tips with approved disinfectant wipes after each patient
options.B: Inspecting the outer plastic casing regularly for cracks or damage
options.C: Storing delicate electronic devices in a clean and dry utility area
options.D: Leaving dirty probes exposed on open countertops between uses

explanation: Thermometer probes must never be left uncleaned or exposed to potential environmental contamination between uses. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T6#BMP112_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of using thermal therapy in clinical practice?

options.A: To replace all forms of medication
options.B: To increase blood pressure rapidly
options.C: To manage pain and promote healing
options.D: To permanently lower body temperature

explanation: Thermal therapy uses heat or cold mainly to relieve discomfort, reduce swelling, and help injured or sore tissues recover. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why do midwives often choose non-pharmacological thermal methods for pregnant or postpartum clients?

options.A: They work faster than any surgical intervention
options.B: They require no assessment of the skin
options.C: They reduce the reliance on pain medications
options.D: They completely cure all types of infections

explanation: Using physical modalities like heat and cold helps manage discomfort safely without introducing unnecessary drugs into the body. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which physiological change occurs immediately when heat is applied to body tissues?

options.A: Immediate freezing of skin cells
options.B: Complete cessation of blood flow
options.C: Vasodilation of local blood vessels
options.D: Severe constriction of capillaries

explanation: Heat causes blood vessels to expand, which increases the flow of blood to the treated area. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h2)

question: A postpartum woman has muscle stiffness in her lower back from labor. Why is applying heat a suitable choice?

options.A: It relaxes muscles and increases blood flow to remove waste
options.B: It immediately shrinks the uterus back to its pre-pregnancy size
options.C: It stops milk production in the mammary glands
options.D: It freezes the nerve endings to stop all sensation forever

explanation: Heat helps tight muscles loosen up and brings blood carrying nutrients to help the sore tissues recover. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is the primary vascular effect of applying a cold pack to fresh tissue trauma?

options.A: Vasodilation
options.B: Vasospasm
options.C: Vascular rupture
options.D: Vasoconstriction

explanation: Cold causes blood vessels to narrow, which reduces blood flow and helps prevent excessive swelling and bleeding. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h3)

question: What happens during the hunting response when cold therapy is left on the skin for too long?

options.A: Muscles begin to contract with maximum force
options.B: Vessels dilate to prevent tissue damage from freezing
options.C: Blood flow stops completely and never returns
options.D: The skin temperature drops below absolute zero

explanation: If cold is applied too long, the body reacts by opening the blood vessels back up to protect the tissue from cold injury. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h3)

question: When is cold therapy generally most appropriate for an episiotomy or perineal tear?

options.A: Only during the active stage of labor
options.B: Whenever the client feels chronic stiffness
options.C: After three weeks of healing
options.D: Within the first twenty-four hours

explanation: Cold is used right after delivery to limit acute swelling and numb the fresh perineal wound. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which of the following conditions is best treated with heat rather than cold?

options.A: Chronic muscle spasms and joint stiffness
options.B: A brand new ankle sprain with heavy swelling
options.C: Active bleeding from a fresh laceration
options.D: An acute bump on the head with active swelling

explanation: Heat helps relax tight muscles and ease long-standing stiffness, whereas fresh injuries need cold to stop swelling. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h4)

question: Why does moist heat generally penetrate deeper into tissues than dry heat?

options.A: Dry heat causes instant skin freezing
options.B: Water is a better thermal conductor than air
options.C: Moisture completely blocks all skin sensation
options.D: Water creates an electrical current in tissue

explanation: Moist applications transfer temperature more efficiently into the body because water conducts heat better than dry materials. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for placing a cloth barrier between an ice pack and a client's skin?

options.A: To warm up the ice before application
options.B: To prevent thermal injury and skin damage
options.C: To increase the weight of the cold pack
options.D: To make the ice pack freeze faster

explanation: Direct contact with extreme temperatures can damage skin cells, so a barrier is necessary for safe application. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h5)

question: What is the recommended maximum time limit for a single thermal therapy session to prevent tissue damage?

options.A: 2 to 3 hours
options.B: 12 to 24 hours
options.C: 15 to 20 minutes
options.D: Continuous 48 hours

explanation: Limiting sessions to fifteen or twenty minutes prevents adverse effects like tissue damage from excessive heat or the hunting response from cold. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why is impaired sensation a strict contraindication for applying heat therapy?

options.A: The client cannot feel if the skin is burning
options.B: Heat will automatically freeze the skin tissue
options.C: The blood vessels will refuse to dilate
options.D: Sensation loss stops all thermal conduction

explanation: If a patient cannot feel temperature properly, they will not be able to warn the midwife if the pack becomes dangerously hot. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h6)

question: Which of the following must be checked on the client's skin BEFORE starting thermal therapy?

options.A: Blood glucose and iron levels
options.B: Integrity, sensation, and temperature
options.C: Cervical dilation and effacement
options.D: Urine output and specific gravity

explanation: The midwife must assess the baseline condition of the skin and its ability to feel temperature before applying hot or cold packs. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h7)

question: A midwife has just finished applying a cold pack to a postpartum client's perineum. What action should be taken next?

options.A: Document the modality, duration, skin condition, and client response
options.B: Immediately apply a high-heat heating pad to reverse the cold
options.C: Leave the cold pack in place continuously for the next three days
options.D: Assume the treatment worked and omit writing notes in the chart

explanation: Proper nursing and midwifery records require noting what was done, how long it lasted, how the skin looked, and if the client felt better. [learn more](BMP112_U4_T7#BMP112_U4_T7_h7)

question: What tiny charged particles move through a wire to create electrical energy?

options.A: Neutrons
options.B: Electrons
options.C: Protons
options.D: Photons

explanation: Electrons are the negatively charged particles that flow through conductors to form an electrical current. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h1)

question: Why is a basic understanding of electricity important for clinical staff in a hospital?

options.A: It helps spot hazards and protect patients from harm
options.B: It allows midwives to repair major internal circuit boards
options.C: It replaces the need for hospital biomedical engineers
options.D: it ensures all medical devices can run without any power source

explanation: Knowing the basics helps clinical staff recognize dangers and safely operate equipment without needing to do complex repairs. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h1)

question: What unit is used to measure electrical voltage?

options.A: Volts
options.B: Amperes
options.C: Watts
options.D: Ohms

explanation: Voltage is measured in volts, representing the electrical potential difference or push in a circuit. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h2)

question: Which everyday system works best as an analogy for voltage?

options.A: The total amount of plastic coating on a power cord
options.B: The physical size and weight of a copper wire
options.C: Water pressure in a pipe pushing fluid forward
options.D: The speed at which a machine consumes electrical power

explanation: Just as water pressure pushes water through a plumbing line, voltage acts as the electrical pressure pushing charges through a wire. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h2)

question: What unit is used to measure electrical current?

options.A: Amperes
options.B: Joules
options.C: Ohms
options.D: Volts

explanation: Current is measured in amperes, which quantify the rate of electron flow through a conductor. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h3)

question: What makes electrical current particularly dangerous to a human patient?

options.A: It can disrupt the normal electrical rhythm of the heart
options.B: It removes all the oxygen molecules from surrounding air
options.C: it causes the voltage in the wall socket to drop to zero
options.D: It instantly melts the protective rubber coating on cables

explanation: Electric current traveling through the body interferes with the heart's natural electrical signals, posing a severe cardiac risk. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h3)

question: What unit is used to measure electrical resistance?

options.A: Watts
options.B: Ohms
options.C: Volts
options.D: Amperes

explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms, representing how much a substance opposes the movement of electrical current. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h4)

question: What happens to human skin resistance when it becomes wet with sweat or saline?

options.A: It increases significantly, blocking all current completely
options.B: It turns the skin into a powerful voltage generator
options.C: It has no effect on how electricity moves through the body
options.D: It drops sharply, increasing the risk of electric shock

explanation: Moisture lowers the skin's electrical resistance, allowing more current to pass through the body if exposed to a live source. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h4)

question: According to Ohm's Law, what happens to current if the electrical resistance increases while voltage stays the same?

options.A: The current stops completely
options.B: The current decreases
options.C: The current increases
options.D: The current remains unchanged

explanation: Resistance opposes flow, so higher resistance results in a lower current for the same amount of voltage. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h5)

question: Which formula correctly represents Ohm's Law for finding current?

options.A: Current equals Voltage divided by Resistance
options.B: Current equals Voltage plus Resistance
options.C: Current equals Voltage multiplied by Resistance
options.D: Current equals Resistance divided by Voltage

explanation: In Ohm's Law, current ($I$) is calculated by dividing voltage ($V$) by resistance ($R$). [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h5)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if a clinical machine sparks or gives a tingling shock?

options.A: Wrap the power cord tightly around the metal frame
options.B: Pour sterile water over the device to cool it down
options.C: Switch it off at the wall socket and unplug it safely
options.D: Continue using it until the end of your shift

explanation: Isolating the power source immediately prevents further injury or fire hazards before reporting the faulty device. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a safe practice when handling medical electrical equipment?

options.A: Inspecting plugs and wires before connecting them to patients
options.B: Using frayed power cords and overloaded multi-plug adapters
options.C: Reporting damaged equipment to the biomedical department
options.D: Keeping electrical devices away from pools of liquid

explanation: Using damaged cords and overloading sockets creates major electrical hazards and must be avoided. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T1#BMP112_U5_T1_h6)

question: What happens to the body's natural resistance to electricity when the skin is broken or wet?

options.A: It increases by a large margin
options.B: It remains completely unchanged
options.C: It decreases significantly
options.D: It fluctuates based on room temperature

explanation: Wet or broken skin lowers the body's electrical resistance, making it much easier for current to enter the body and cause harm. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why are clinical environments considered more electrically hazardous than normal offices?

options.A: Medical equipment is built with cheap and unsafe industrial materials
options.B: Patients often have medical lines directly connected inside their bodies
options.C: Hospital electrical systems carry a much higher voltage than standard homes
options.D: Clinical staff rarely receive training on basic electrical safety rules

explanation: Invasive lines like pacemakers or IV catheters bypass the skin barrier, creating direct pathways for electrical current to reach internal organs. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which type of electrical shock can be triggered by an extremely tiny current flowing directly to the heart?

options.A: Thermal shock
options.B: Static shock
options.C: Macroshock
options.D: Microshock

explanation: A microshock involves a very small current that bypasses the skin and flows straight to the heart, posing a severe risk to vulnerable patients. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h2)

question: What makes a microshock particularly dangerous compared to a standard macroshock?

options.A: It produces visible burns on the outer surface of the patient's skin
options.B: It always trips the main circuit breaker before anyone notices
options.C: It requires very little current to cause a fatal heart rhythm disturbance
options.D: It only occurs when high-voltage X-ray machines malfunction

explanation: Because the current goes directly to the heart via internal lines, even a microscopic amount of electricity can disrupt the heart rhythm. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of a ground wire in clinical electrical equipment?

options.A: To provide a safe, low-resistance path for fault current into the earth
options.B: To speed up the battery charging time of portable medical devices
options.C: To prevent the equipment from overheating during long procedures
options.D: To increase the total electrical voltage delivered to the machine

explanation: The ground wire diverts stray electrical current safely away from users and patients and into the ground. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h3)

question: What should clinical staff do immediately if the line isolation monitor alarm goes off in an operating room?

options.A: Ignore the alarm because isolated power systems prevent any risk of electric shock
options.B: Disconnect all surgical lights and wait for the municipal power company to arrive
options.C: Recognize that a single electrical fault has occurred and investigate the equipment
options.D: Evacuate the entire building because the main power grid has failed completely

explanation: An isolated power monitor alarm warns of a first-fault condition; equipment continues running safely, but staff must identify the faulty device. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h3)

question: What action should you take first when you notice a frayed power cord on an infusion pump?

options.A: Continue using it until the end of your current shift
options.B: Wrap the frayed section tightly with ordinary adhesive tape
options.C: Plug it into a different wall socket to reduce the risk
options.D: Remove the pump from service and label it as broken

explanation: Damaged equipment must be taken out of use immediately and tagged to prevent accidental use by other staff members. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h4)

question: Why are routine checks by biomedical engineering departments necessary in hospitals?

options.A: To ensure that all medical devices use the exact same brand of power cord
options.B: To detect hidden electrical faults and leakage currents before accidents happen
options.C: To comply with paperwork rules without affecting actual clinical work
options.D: To increase the resale value of old clinical equipment over time

explanation: Regular technical testing catches internal deterioration and current leakage that cannot be seen during a simple visual check. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h4)

question: What is the FIRST action a nurse should take when discovering someone attached to a live electrical source?

options.A: Grab the patient's hands firmly and pull them away from the machine
options.B: Run out of the room immediately to look for a fire extinguisher
options.C: Pour cold water over the electrical equipment to cool down the wires
options.D: Cut off the power source or safely separate the person using a non-conductive object

explanation: You must break the electrical contact first to prevent the current from flowing through you and injuring you as well. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h5)

question: Why is it dangerous to touch a patient who is actively receiving an electric shock from faulty equipment?

options.A: It will cause the hospital's main water pipes to burst
options.B: The electrical current can flow through the rescuer's body
options.C: It automatically triggers the fire alarm throughout the ward
options.D: The patient's skin will become permanently stained by the current

explanation: Human bodies conduct electricity well, meaning a rescuer touching a victim in contact with a live circuit will also receive a shock. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T2#BMP112_U5_T2_h5)

question: What is the typical electrical charge inside a resting cell compared to the outside?

options.A: Positive
options.B: Negative
options.C: Fluctuating
options.D: Neutral

explanation: Cells maintain a resting membrane potential where the inside is more negative than the outside due to ion distribution. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h1)

question: What makes the inside of a cell turn positive during an action potential?

options.A: Calcium ions dissolving in the cytoplasm
options.B: Potassium ions leaving the cell rapidly
options.C: Chloride ions accumulating at the membrane
options.D: Sodium ions rushing inside the cell

explanation: When an excitable cell is stimulated, sodium channels open and sodium ions flood into the cell, reversing the local charge. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which part of the heart's conduction system acts as the primary natural pacemaker?

options.A: Atrioventricular node
options.B: Bundle of His
options.C: Sinoatrial node
options.D: Purkinje fibers

explanation: The sinoatrial node sets the normal pace of the heart by spontaneously generating electrical impulses. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h2)

question: What does the QRS complex on an ECG tracing represent?

options.A: Depolarization of the atria
options.B: Repolarization of the ventricles
options.C: Depolarization of the ventricles
options.D: Repolarization of the atria

explanation: The QRS complex corresponds to the electrical activation and contraction of the large ventricular muscles. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h2)

question: How many physical electrodes are placed on a patient for a standard 12-lead ECG?

options.A: Ten
options.B: Six
options.C: Fourteen
options.D: Twelve

explanation: A standard 12-lead ECG uses 10 physical cables and electrodes to calculate 12 different electrical viewing angles. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h3)

question: Why is correct placement of chest electrodes important during an ECG recording?

options.A: Incorrect positions drain the battery of the monitoring equipment
options.B: Incorrect placement can distort waveform shapes and lead to misdiagnoses
options.C: Misplaced electrodes prevent the machine from turning on at all
options.D: Wrong placement causes painful electrical shocks to the patient

explanation: Accurate lead placement ensures that the recorded electrical vectors truly reflect the electrical activity of specific heart regions. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h3)

question: What is a single motor unit made up of?

options.A: An entire skeletal muscle and its main blood supply
options.B: Two adjacent muscle fibers sharing a cell membrane
options.C: A motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it supplies
options.D: A group of sensory nerves attached to a tendon

explanation: A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron together with every muscle fiber it activates. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of recording motor unit action potentials during an EMG test?

options.A: To calculate the total body fat percentage of the limbs
options.B: To monitor fetal heart rate variations during contractions
options.C: To distinguish between muscle disorders and nerve injuries
options.D: To measure the exact cardiac output of the patient

explanation: Examining motor unit action potentials helps locate the source of neuromuscular weakness. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common source of electrical artifact in bioelectric recordings?

options.A: Intact intracellular potassium balance
options.B: Respiratory chest wall movement
options.C: Mains electrical power line interference
options.D: Patient muscle tremors and shivering

explanation: Intracellular ion balance is a normal physiological state, whereas tremors, breathing, and power lines cause external recording artifacts. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h5)

question: How does preparing the skin before applying ECG or EMG electrodes improve signal quality?

options.A: It increases the voltage output of the heart automatically
options.B: It sterilizes the skin to prevent systemic bacterial infections
options.C: It lowers skin resistance and reduces interference artifacts
options.D: It warms up the underlying muscle fibers for faster action potentials

explanation: Cleaning oils and dead skin cells improves electrical contact, ensuring a cleaner trace with fewer baseline disturbances. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T3#BMP112_U5_T3_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying an external electrical current to the heart during an emergency?

options.A: To permanently stop all electrical impulses in the cardiac muscle
options.B: To increase the overall strength of the heart's pumping action
options.C: To permanently replace the natural pacemaker cells in the heart
options.D: To reset chaotic electrical activity and restore a normal rhythm

explanation: An emergency shock depolarizes the heart cells simultaneously, which stops the abnormal rhythm and gives the natural pacemaker a chance to take over. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why does ventricular fibrillation require immediate electrical intervention?

options.A: The heart rate becomes too slow to maintain adequate blood pressure
options.B: The natural pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial node have completely died
options.C: The coronary arteries instantly block and cause a massive heart attack
options.D: The heart stops pumping blood effectively because its chambers quiver instead of beating

explanation: During ventricular fibrillation, the ventricles quiver uselessly rather than contracting, meaning no blood is pumped to the brain and body. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h1)

question: How does a biphasic defibrillation waveform differ from a monophasic waveform?

options.A: It delivers electricity continuously over a much longer time period
options.B: It requires significantly higher energy settings to work properly
options.C: It uses alternating current instead of direct current energy
options.D: It reverses the direction of the electrical current during delivery

explanation: Biphasic shocks send current in one direction and then switch it back, which is gentler on the heart tissue and requires fewer joules. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h2)

question: Where should defibrillator pads generally be placed on the patient's chest to ensure the current passes through the heart?

options.A: One pad on the upper right sternum and the other at the left apex
options.B: Both pads placed underneath the left armpit near the shoulder blade
options.C: Both pads placed tightly together directly over the center of the sternum
options.D: One pad on the upper back and the other on the lower right abdomen

explanation: This standard placement ensures the electrical pathway travels directly across the ventricular mass of the heart. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following cardiac rhythms is appropriate for emergency defibrillation?

options.A: Pulseless electrical activity
options.B: Sinus bradycardia
options.C: Ventricular asystole
options.D: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia

explanation: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are the only two shockable cardiac arrest rhythms. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h3)

question: What immediate action should the midwifery team take after delivering a shock to a patient in ventricular fibrillation?

options.A: Resume chest compressions immediately without checking for a pulse
options.B: Administer a dose of intravenous calcium gluconate
options.C: Wait two full minutes while watching the monitor for a normal sinus rhythm
options.D: Check the patient's blood pressure using an automated cuff

explanation: Resuscitation guidelines emphasize restarting chest compressions right away to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion, delaying rhythm checks. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary function of an artificial cardiac pacemaker?

options.A: To physically pump blood through the lungs and systemic circulation
options.B: To shock the heart out of dangerous life-threatening ventricular rhythms
options.C: To deliver electrical impulses when the natural heart rate is too slow
options.D: To measure the exact oxygen saturation levels inside the heart chambers

explanation: Pacemakers step in to pace the heart when the intrinsic rate falls below acceptable limits, unlike defibrillators which treat cardiac arrest. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h4)

question: What are the two main physical components that make up an artificial pacemaker system?

options.A: A battery charger and a wireless handheld tablet
options.B: A mechanical valve and a flexible plastic reservoir
options.C: External gel pads and a manual charging handle
options.D: A pulse generator and insulated leads

explanation: The pulse generator houses the battery and computer brain, while the leads carry the electrical signal from the generator into the heart tissue. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h4)

question: When is a temporary pacemaker typically chosen over a permanent implanted device?

options.A: For patients who require lifelong management of chronic heart block
options.B: For routine prevention of sudden cardiac arrest in healthy adults
options.C: For acute and reversible heart rhythm problems
options.D: For individuals who participate in high-impact athletic activities

explanation: Temporary pacing is used short-term when a slow heart rhythm is expected to resolve, such as after an acute drug overdose or heart attack. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h5)

question: Where is a permanent pacemaker pulse generator most commonly placed during surgical implantation?

options.A: Beneath the skin of the upper thigh near the groin
options.B: Under the skin in the pectoral chest area
options.C: On the outer surface of the left arm near the elbow
options.D: Directly inside the abdominal cavity near the liver

explanation: The subcutaneous pocket in the upper chest near the collarbone is the standard anatomical site for permanent pacemaker placement. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h5)

question: What visual sign on a cardiac monitor indicates that a pacemaker has successfully fired an electrical impulse?

options.A: A rapid oscillation of the baseline
options.B: A sudden drop in the heart rate
options.C: A wide and irregular flat line
options.D: A sharp vertical spike on the tracing

explanation: Pacing spikes appear as thin, vertical lines on the rhythm strip right before the heart muscle responds with a P wave or QRS complex. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is an important instruction for a patient living with a new permanent pacemaker?

options.A: Avoid strong magnetic fields and report symptoms like dizziness
options.B: Refrain from moving the left arm entirely for the rest of life
options.C: Stop taking all prescribed cardiac medications immediately
options.D: Check and record your blood pressure once every three weeks

explanation: Strong magnets, such as those in MRI machines or industrial equipment, can interfere with pacemaker programming and should be avoided. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h6)

question: What does 'failure to capture' mean when monitoring a patient with a pacemaker?

options.A: Pacing spikes appear on the monitor, but the heart muscle fails to contract
options.B: The generator has shifted out of the subcutaneous chest pocket
options.C: The pacemaker battery is completely dead and shows no electrical spikes
options.D: The heart beats too fast and the device fails to slow it down

explanation: Failure to capture occurs when the electrical stimulus delivered by the pacemaker is not strong enough to trigger depolarization of the myocardium. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h7)

question: Which complication happens when a pacemaker fails to recognize the heart's own natural electrical activity and fires at inappropriate times?

options.A: Failure to sense
options.B: Battery depletion
options.C: Failure to capture
options.D: Lead displacement

explanation: Under-sensing or failure to sense means the device cannot detect intrinsic beats, leading to unnecessary and potentially dangerous pacing spikes. [learn more](BMP112_U5_T4#BMP112_U5_T4_h7)

question: What type of energy does an ultrasound machine use to create images inside the body?

options.A: Visible light spectrum rays
options.B: Strong magnetic field pulses
options.C: Ionizing radiation beams
options.D: High-frequency sound waves

explanation: Ultrasound imaging operates entirely on acoustic energy using high-frequency sound waves rather than harmful radiation. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h1)

question: Why is ultrasonography generally preferred over standard X-rays for routine pregnancy evaluations?

options.A: It costs nothing to maintain the machine
options.B: It does not use ionizing radiation
options.C: It provides full color permanent pictures
options.D: It requires zero training for operators

explanation: Avoiding ionizing radiation makes ultrasound safe for routine monitoring of a growing fetus during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h1)

question: What physical requirement is mandatory for sound waves to travel from one point to another?

options.A: A magnetic field
options.B: A complete vacuum
options.C: A physical medium
options.D: An electric current

explanation: Sound waves are mechanical vibrations that must travel through matter and cannot move through empty space. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h2)

question: Which of the following describes the relationship between ultrasound frequency and depth penetration?

options.A: Lower frequencies offer sharper details
options.B: Higher frequencies reach deeper organs
options.C: Higher frequencies penetrate less deep
options.D: Frequency has no effect on penetration

explanation: High-frequency waves give high resolution but are easily absorbed, meaning they cannot travel deep into tissues. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h2)

question: What primary job does the piezoelectric crystal perform inside an ultrasound probe?

options.A: Convert energy between electrical and sound waves
options.B: Display the final picture on the monitor screen
options.C: Generate ionizing radiation for deep imaging
options.D: Store power from the main electrical outlet

explanation: Piezoelectric crystals swap electrical currents into mechanical sound pulses and change returning echoes back into electrical signals. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h3)

question: What happens when an electrical voltage is applied directly to a piezoelectric crystal inside a transducer?

options.A: It emits a burst of light rays
options.B: It vibrates to emit a sound wave
options.C: It melts from high internal heat
options.D: It turns completely invisible

explanation: Applying electricity causes the crystal to change shape rapidly, creating the mechanical pressure wave known as sound. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h3)

question: What does acoustic impedance measure in biological tissues?

options.A: Total electrical charge of cells
options.B: Resistance to the passage of sound
options.C: Amount of iron stored in blood
options.D: Speed of blood flow in vessels

explanation: Acoustic impedance tells us how difficult it is for sound waves to travel through a specific type of body tissue. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h4)

question: Why does a large echo occur when a sound wave hits the boundary between two tissues with very different acoustic impedances?

options.A: The tissues absorb all acoustic energy
options.B: A sharp mismatch causes strong reflection
options.C: The sound wave speeds up infinitely
options.D: The crystals inside the probe break

explanation: Great differences in acoustic impedance at tissue borders force a high percentage of the sound wave to bounce back as an echo. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h4)

question: What term describes the gradual loss of ultrasound beam intensity as it travels deeper into body tissues?

options.A: Piezoelectric
options.B: Refraction
options.C: Impedance
options.D: Attenuation

explanation: Attenuation is the overall reduction in sound wave strength as it travels, gets absorbed, and scatters through tissues. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a primary cause of ultrasound wave attenuation in the body?

options.A: Instant amplification of returning echoes
options.B: Absorption of acoustic energy as heat
options.C: Beam divergence over long distances
options.D: Scattering of sound by small structures

explanation: Amplification increases signal strength on the screen; it does not cause sound waves to weaken inside the body. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h5)

question: Which ultrasound display mode produces the standard 2D grayscale anatomical pictures used during routine antenatal scans?

options.A: B-Mode
options.B: A-Mode
options.C: Z-Mode
options.D: M-Mode

explanation: B-Mode translates echo amplitudes into bright and dark dots to form a spatial two-dimensional image of body organs. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h6)

question: A midwife wants to evaluate the rapid movement and rhythm of an early fetal heartbeat on a moving graph line. Which ultrasound mode should be selected?

options.A: A-Mode
options.B: X-Mode
options.C: M-Mode
options.D: Static Mode

explanation: Motion mode charts structural movement over time along a scrolling graph, making it perfect for checking fetal heart rates. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h6)

question: What safety principle guides clinicians to keep ultrasound exposure times and power outputs as low as possible?

options.A: ALARA principle
options.B: PIEZO protocol
options.C: DOPPLER rule
options.D: OMEGA standard

explanation: The ALARA principle ensures that energy exposure is kept As Low As Reasonably Achievable during any diagnostic scan. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h7)

question: Why is adhering to safety guidelines regarding acoustic output important even though ultrasound lacks ionizing radiation?

options.A: Prolonged scanning permanently drains the machine battery
options.B: Excessive probe pressure can cause immediate fetal distress
options.C: High-intensity sound waves can cause tissue heating and cavitation
options.D: Sound waves can turn into dangerous X-rays inside the uterus

explanation: Intense acoustic energy can produce localized tissue heating or microscopic bubble formation, requiring prudent use. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T1#BMP112_U6_T1_h7)

question: What are the individual packets of light energy called?

options.A: Photons
options.B: Neutrons
options.C: Electrons
options.D: Protons

explanation: Light is made up of discrete packets of energy called photons. These packets interact with matter when light is absorbed. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h1)

question: Why do midwives and nurses need to know how light behaves in medical devices?

options.A: It determines how fast sound travels through fetal tissue
options.B: It explains how light-based clinical devices like pulse oximeters work
options.C: It helps calculate the exact dosage of light therapy for jaundice
options.D: It prevents damage to the retina during standard visual acuity tests

explanation: Medical devices such as pulse oximeters rely on how light energy is absorbed by tissue, linking physics concepts directly to bedside monitoring. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which behavior of light causes rays to bend when passing from air into the cornea?

options.A: Scattering
options.B: Refraction
options.C: Diffraction
options.D: Reflection

explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it moves from one transparent medium into another with a different density. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h2)

question: What happens to light rays during scattering inside a medium?

options.A: They deviate in multiple random directions
options.B: They bounce off at an equal opposite angle
options.C: They speed up significantly beyond the speed of light
options.D: They stop moving completely and turn into heat

explanation: Scattering causes light to spread out in various directions when it hits particles or rough surfaces, unlike clean reflection. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h2)

question: What is the unit of measurement used for the optical focusing power of the eye?

options.A: Lumens
options.B: Millimeters
options.C: Diopters
options.D: Decibels

explanation: Optical power, especially for lenses and the eye, is measured in diopters. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h3)

question: How does the lens inside the eye change shape to focus on near objects?

options.A: It flattens
options.B: It thickens
options.C: It detaches from the supporting fibers
options.D: It shrinks in length

explanation: When viewing objects up close, the ciliary muscles contract, causing the elastic lens to become thicker to increase its focusing power. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h3)

question: Which type of lens is used to correct myopia, or nearsightedness?

options.A: Convex lens
options.B: Concave lens
options.C: Cylindrical lens
options.D: Prism lens

explanation: Concave lenses spread light rays out slightly before they enter the eye, moving the focal point back onto the retina for nearsighted individuals. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h4)

question: An older pregnant woman reports that reading close-up charts has become difficult due to the natural aging of her eye lenses. What condition is this?

options.A: Astigmatism
options.B: Myopia
options.C: Presbyopia
options.D: Cataracts

explanation: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation caused by the hardening of the lens, making close-up work difficult. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h4)

question: Which clinical instrument is used to examine the retina and blood vessels at the back of the eye?

options.A: Stethoscope
options.B: Sphygmomanometer
options.C: Otoscope
options.D: Ophthalmoscope

explanation: An ophthalmoscope uses built-in lighting and magnifying lenses to inspect the internal structures of the eye, including the retina. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h5)

question: Why is light therapy used for newborns with neonatal jaundice?

options.A: It breaks down excess bilirubin in the skin through photo-oxidation
options.B: It disinfects the surface of the infant's skin
options.C: It stimulates the production of red blood cells in the liver
options.D: It improves the visual acuity of premature infants

explanation: Phototherapy uses light waves to transform bilirubin into forms that the baby's body can easily excrete. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T2#BMP112_U6_T2_h5)

question: What are the small individual packets of energy that make up light called?

options.A: Electrons
options.B: Neutrons
options.C: Chromophores
options.D: Photons

explanation: Light is made up of small packets of energy known as photons, which interact directly with body tissues during light-based therapies. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h1)

question: Why is the absorption of light by chromophores important in medical treatments?

options.A: It completely stops all light waves from reflecting off the skin's surface
options.B: It turns the targeted biological tissue completely invisible to the human eye
options.C: It allows specific wavelengths of light energy to target and affect particular tissues
options.D: It prevents any thermal energy from building up inside the patient's body

explanation: Chromophores absorb specific light wavelengths, which is what lets medical treatments target exact cells or molecules without harming surrounding areas. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h1)

question: What does the word monochromatic mean when describing a laser beam?

options.A: It carries an extremely high electrical voltage
options.B: It consists of a single wavelength or color
options.C: All of its light waves move completely in phase
options.D: It travels in a straight and parallel path

explanation: Monochromatic literally means one color, meaning the laser emits light of a single, precise wavelength. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h2)

question: What is the main job of the optical cavity mirrors inside a medical laser device?

options.A: To change the electrical current directly into a visible colored beam
options.B: To protect the operator from accidental exposure to harmful radiation
options.C: To bounce the light back and forth to amplify the beam before release
options.D: To cool down the active medium so the machine does not overheat

explanation: The mirrors trap and bounce the light through the active medium, building up the intensity of the beam before letting it escape through the output mirror. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h2)

question: Which medical laser is known for being absorbed by water and used for precise cutting?

options.A: Ultraviolet-B laser
options.B: Argon laser
options.C: Low-level laser
options.D: Carbon dioxide (CO2) laser

explanation: The CO2 laser is heavily absorbed by cellular water, making it extremely effective for precise surgical cutting and vaporization. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h3)

question: Which type of laser is most appropriate when a doctor needs a beam absorbed by blood vessels?

options.A: Carbon dioxide laser
options.B: Low-level therapy laser
options.C: Argon laser
options.D: Infrared heating lamp

explanation: Argon lasers emit light that is strongly absorbed by hemoglobin, making them ideal for treating delicate vascular structures. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h3)

question: Which ultraviolet band has the shortest wavelength and is used for sterilization?

options.A: UVA
options.B: UVC
options.C: Visible light
options.D: UVB

explanation: UVC radiation has the shortest wavelength and highest energy, making it lethal to microorganisms and ideal for disinfection. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h4)

question: Why is ultraviolet light generally invisible to the human eye?

options.A: Its wavelengths fall outside the normal visible light spectrum range
options.B: It travels too fast for the retinal cells to process the incoming photons
options.C: Its energy packets lack the necessary intensity to trigger optical nerves
options.D: It is completely absorbed by the outermost layer of the human cornea

explanation: Human vision is limited to a specific range of wavelengths, and UV light sits outside this band, just beyond violet light. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h4)

question: How does germicidal UVC light successfully kill or inactivate microorganisms?

options.A: By removing all the oxygen molecules from the surrounding air
options.B: By turning the intracellular fluid into an acidic solution
options.C: By melting their outer cell walls through intense thermal heat
options.D: By damaging their DNA and preventing them from replicating

explanation: UVC light disrupts microbial DNA structure, stopping germs from dividing and rendering them harmless. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h5)

question: A newborn baby in the ward develops physiological jaundice. Which light-based intervention helps clear the bilirubin?

options.A: Continuous exposure to germicidal UVC lamps positioned directly over the infant's cot
options.B: Targeted ultraviolet-A radiation to darken the skin pigment and mask the yellow color
options.C: Phototherapy using specific light wavelengths to change bilirubin into a water-soluble form
options.D: Deep-tissue heating using an infrared surgical laser to stimulate liver enzymes

explanation: Phototherapy units break down toxic bilirubin in the baby's skin into water-soluble forms that can be readily excreted. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h5)

question: What is a major fire hazard associated with the use of surgical lasers in the operating theatre?

options.A: They routinely cause electrical wiring inside the walls to melt
options.B: They heat up the entire room air until ceiling fans catch fire
options.C: They cause flammable cleaning liquids stored in cupboards to explode
options.D: They can ignite surgical drapes, prep solutions, and oxygen tubing

explanation: Surgical lasers are powerful heat sources that can easily ignite flammable items like drapes, oxygen supplies, and alcohol-based skin preps. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h6)

question: Why is it dangerous for surgical staff to rely on standard sunglasses when working around medical lasers?

options.A: The high heat from the laser will melt standard plastic sunglasses instantly
options.B: Standard sunglasses do not block the specific, intense wavelengths of the laser beam being used
options.C: Standard sunglasses are too dark and prevent the surgical team from seeing the patient
options.D: Standard sunglasses will reflect the laser beam directly back into the sterile surgical wound

explanation: Laser safety goggles are engineered to filter out precise optical wavelengths, whereas regular sunglasses lack this targeted protection and offer a false sense of security. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T3#BMP112_U6_T3_h6)

question: Name the scientist who discovered X-rays in 1895.

options.A: Wilhelm Röntgen
options.B: Alexander Fleming
options.C: Marie Curie
options.D: Albert Einstein

explanation: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, changing the face of modern medical diagnostics forever. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h1)

question: What is the primary medical benefit of using X-rays in clinical practice?

options.A: Viewing internal body structures without surgery
options.B: Measuring the exact electrical activity of the heart
options.C: Destroying harmful bacteria on the skin surface
options.D: Treating chronic high blood pressure conditions

explanation: X-rays allow healthcare providers to look inside the human body non-invasively to check bones and organs. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h1)

question: Which metal is commonly used as the target in an X-ray tube anode?

options.A: Aluminum
options.B: Copper
options.C: Iron
options.D: Tungsten

explanation: Tungsten is chosen because it has a very high melting point and can withstand the intense heat generated by bombarding electrons. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h2)

question: Where do X-rays fall on the electromagnetic spectrum relative to visible light?

options.A: Lower frequency and longer wavelength
options.B: Higher frequency and shorter wavelength
options.C: Higher frequency and longer wavelength
options.D: Lower frequency and shorter wavelength

explanation: X-rays have much shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies than visible light, giving them greater penetrating power. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h2)

question: What term describes tissues that allow X-ray beams to pass through them easily?

options.A: Refractive
options.B: Radiolucent
options.C: Resilient
options.D: Radiopaque

explanation: Radiolucent structures, like lungs filled with air, offer little resistance to X-rays and show up dark on radiographs. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h3)

question: Why do bones appear white on a standard X-ray image?

options.A: They stain the X-ray film a milky white color
options.B: They emit their own bright light when exposed
options.C: They absorb or block most of the X-ray photons
options.D: They let all the radiation pass straight through

explanation: Dense bone tissue blocks the X-rays from hitting the film or digital plate behind it, creating a white shadow. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which of the five basic radiographic densities appears the darkest on an X-ray film?

options.A: Metal
options.B: Bone
options.C: Air
options.D: Fat

explanation: Air offers zero resistance to the beam, so maximum X-rays reach the film to produce a black appearance. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h4)

question: A patient swallows a metallic coin. How will this object most likely appear on an X-ray?

options.A: Transparent blue
options.B: Pitch black
options.C: Intermediate gray
options.D: Bright white

explanation: Metal is extremely dense and blocks almost all X-ray photons, showing up as a very bright white shape on the image. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h4)

question: What does the acronym ALARA stand for in radiation safety?

options.A: As Low As Reasonably Achievable
options.B: Always Leave Area Radiologically Active
options.C: Avoid Lead Aprons Risking Accidents
options.D: As Little Absorption Rates Allow

explanation: ALARA is the golden rule of radiation protection, ensuring patients receive only the minimum necessary dose. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h5)

question: Why is special caution required when considering X-rays for a pregnant woman?

options.A: Pregnancy turns all soft tissues completely radiopaque
options.B: Radiation causes the ultrasound equipment to malfunction
options.C: Developing fetal cells are sensitive to ionizing radiation
options.D: X-ray machines do not work properly on pregnant bodies

explanation: Rapidly dividing cells in a developing fetus are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of ionizing radiation. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common reason to perform a chest X-ray in clinical practice?

options.A: Checking for cardiac chamber enlargement
options.B: Monitoring active labor contractions
options.C: Screening for pulmonary tuberculosis
options.D: Evaluating a persistent chronic cough

explanation: Chest X-rays evaluate the heart and lungs, not uterine contractions, which are monitored via palpation or electronic fetal monitoring. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h6)

question: Why do plain X-rays remain widely used in resource-limited healthcare settings across Nigeria?

options.A: They are relatively fast, affordable, and accessible
options.B: They are completely harmless to a developing fetus
options.C: They provide clearer 3D color images than MRIs
options.D: They do not use any form of ionizing radiation

explanation: Plain radiographs offer a reliable, cost-effective diagnostic option where advanced imaging machines are scarce. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T4#BMP112_U6_T4_h6)

question: Where inside an atom do gamma rays come from?

options.A: In the outermost electron shell
options.B: Within the surrounding magnetic field
options.C: Inside the atomic nucleus
options.D: Between molecular binding sites

explanation: Gamma rays are released from changes inside the nucleus of a radioactive atom. X-rays, by contrast, come from electrons outside the nucleus. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h1)

question: How are gamma rays different from sound waves?

options.A: Sound waves carry ionizing energy particles
options.B: Gamma rays can only move through solid objects
options.C: Gamma rays travel without needing a physical medium
options.D: Sound waves have a much higher frequency than gamma rays

explanation: Electromagnetic waves like gamma rays can travel through empty space. Sound waves require a solid, liquid, or gas medium to move. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h1)

question: What happens to an atom's nucleus when it gives off a gamma ray?

options.A: It drops from an excited state to a stable state
options.B: It gains an extra proton from the surrounding tissue
options.C: It loses two neutrons through nuclear fission
options.D: It converts completely into a different chemical element

explanation: Gamma emission rids the nucleus of excess energy without changing the number of protons or neutrons, leaving the element the same. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h2)

question: Which type of radioactive decay usually happens right before gamma rays are released?

options.A: Alpha or beta decay
options.B: Ultraviolet photolysis
options.C: Nuclear fusion bonding
options.D: Electron capture ionization

explanation: Atomic nuclei often stay in an unstable, excited energy state right after ejecting alpha or beta particles, causing them to release gamma rays next. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h2)

question: What is the electric charge of a gamma photon?

options.A: Negative charge
options.B: Positive charge
options.C: Dual fluctuating charge
options.D: Neutral charge

explanation: Gamma rays are pure electromagnetic energy with no electrical charge, which means magnetic fields cannot bend or deflect them. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h3)

question: Why do gamma rays need dense materials like lead to block them?

options.A: They react instantly with air to create electrical sparks
options.B: They attract magnetic metals and destroy them on contact
options.C: They have high penetrating power and pass easily through light materials
options.D: They carry heavy physical mass that breaks down thin barriers

explanation: Because they lack mass and charge, gamma rays pass right through low-density matter. Very dense atoms packed closely together are needed to absorb them. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h3)

question: Why is a developing fetus especially sensitive to gamma radiation?

options.A: Fetal bone structures absorb all gamma rays like a sponge
options.B: Fetal tissues contain rapidly dividing cells that are easily damaged
options.C: Unborn babies lack any cellular repair mechanisms whatsoever
options.D: The amniotic fluid accelerates the speed of gamma photons

explanation: Tissues with high rates of cell division sustain much more permanent disruption from ionizing radiation, placing a pregnancy at high risk. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h4)

question: What is the main way gamma rays cause damage to living cells?

options.A: By raising the overall body temperature until proteins melt
options.B: By ionizing atoms and breaking molecular bonds like DNA
options.C: By draining all the water content out of the cell membrane
options.D: By blocking oxygen from binding to hemoglobin molecules

explanation: The intense energy of gamma photons strips electrons from atoms, creating chemical instability that directly damages vital genetic material. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h4)

question: Which medical device uses focused gamma rays to treat brain tumors without open surgery?

options.A: Ultrasound probe
options.B: Dialysis machine
options.C: Gamma Knife
options.D: Infusion pump

explanation: The Gamma Knife focuses many low-intensity gamma beams from different angles onto a precise point to destroy tumor cells without traditional surgery. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of using radioactive tracers in diagnostic imaging?

options.A: To freeze blood flow so doctors can take clear pictures
options.B: To physically burn away diseased tissue from inside the organ
options.C: To emit gamma rays that external cameras map to view organ function
options.D: To provide nutritional energy to failing cells in the body

explanation: Tracers emit safe levels of gamma rays from inside the body, allowing specialized cameras to detect blood flow and metabolic activity. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three core principles of radiation safety?

options.A: Speed
options.B: Distance
options.C: Shielding
options.D: Time

explanation: The standard radiation protection rules are time, distance, and shielding. Moving faster does not reduce radiation exposure doses. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T5#BMP112_U6_T5_h6)

question: Why do healthcare workers wear personal dosimeter badges in units with radiation sources?

options.A: To prove to patients that the equipment has been turned off
options.B: To track their cumulative radiation exposure over a working period
options.C: To block incoming gamma rays from striking their chest area
options.D: To sound an alarm when a radioactive patient enters the room

question: What is the main danger of ionizing radiation to human cells?

options.A: Damage to cellular DNA
options.B: Rapid cooling of tissue
options.C: Permanent muscle wasting
options.D: Depletion of body water

question: Why should healthcare workers in Nigerian hospitals be careful about radiation exposure?

options.A: Radiation effects add up over time with ongoing exposure
options.B: Patients become radioactive and dangerous after a simple scan
options.C: Medical imaging units generate toxic chemical fumes daily
options.D: X-ray equipment frequently explodes if left plugged in

explanation: Even low doses of radiation can accumulate over years of clinical work, so safe handling practices are essential to prevent long-term cellular damage. [learn more](BMP112_U6_T6#BMP112_U6_T6_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the three main rules of radiation protection?

options.C: Shielding

question: How does stepping further away from an active mobile X-ray machine affect your radiation exposure?

options.B: It lowers your dose because radiation intensity drops with distance
options.C: It increases your dose because radiation bounces off walls
options.D: It stops all radiation waves instantly

question: What is the recommended annual radiation dose limit for a healthcare worker, averaged over five years?

question: Why is there no fixed maximum dose limit for patients having X-ray procedures?

options.B: Medical exposures are based on clinical need and kept as low as possible
options.C: Patients are naturally immune to radiation
options.D: Diagnostic imaging machines do not produce enough energy to harm patients

question: Where should a healthcare worker wear their radiation dosimeter badge during fluoroscopy?

question: What is the correct way to store lead aprons in a clinical department?

options.D: Folded neatly into a square on a shelf

question: Why is confirming pregnancy status important before scheduling diagnostic imaging?

options.C: Radiographers refuse to work without a signed certificate
options.D: Pregnant women are legally barred from radiology suites

question: What should a nurse do when a mobile X-ray machine is about to be used in a shared ward?

question: Which agency is responsible for regulating radiation safety and licensing medical X-ray facilities in Nigeria?

question: Why do Nigerian hospitals appoint a Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)?
